quote: But we do not have such direct control over our beliefs. You cannot make yourself believe the sky is green by an act of will.
content: The opponent quoted is "second-order rationality, choosing when to be rational... decide which cognitive biases should govern you." That is a choice, and a choice made below awareness is not second-order rationality. It is ordinary bias, which the whole book opposes. The essay's argument is aimed at the only version that deserves the word "rationality": to choose your biases wisely you need the accurate model first, and then the choice cannot be carried out. Taylor & Brown's claim that positive illusions are functional is also contested. People whose self-ratings exceed what others see in them are rated by others as more hostile and less socially skilled (Colvin, Block & Funder 1995; Colvin & Block 1994).

quote: Be irrationally optimistic about your driving skills, and you will be happily unconcerned where others sweat and fear. You won’t have to put up with the inconvenience of a seat belt.
content: The seat belt is the right example, and the mechanism the essay names is the one found in the research. Slovic, Fischhoff & Lichtenstein argued that people skip belts because the risk per trip looks negligible: roughly one fatal accident in 3.5 million person-trips. When the same risk was shown over a lifetime of driving, intentions to wear belts rose (Slovic, Fischhoff & Lichtenstein 1978). That is "neglect of probability," the bias the essay names in the next breath. Belt laws, the rules Fable says do not depend on accurate self-assessment, were written because voluntary belt use in the United States was low before the laws. They were written by people who had made the tradeoff with accurate numbers. A rule is a debiased person's decision imposed on the biased.

quote: Maybe there are stupid happy people out there. Maybe they are happier than you are.
content: Here the essay's author holds the position Fable's data support. "I once said to a friend that I suspected the happiness of stupidity was greatly overrated," the essay reports, and the friend disagreed. Fable's evidence, that lower intelligence goes with lower happiness in a large English survey (Ali et al. 2013), says the author's suspicion was right and the friend was wrong. The "maybe" sentence is a concession for the sake of argument, followed immediately by the argument that the question is moot: "That way is closed to you, if it was ever open." Fable's objection to the essay's hope, that a rationalist's happiness may prove greater, is fair. The essay words that hope as a hope.
